title: Learning and labor (Avot 2:2)
hook: study joined with work is good; together they keep wrongdoing away

segments.voice: Yesterday, an eye that sees, an ear that hears, and a book where it's all written. Your line was the ear hears. What did you catch yourself saying under your breath? Day two hundred fifty-one.

There are two ways to get stuck. One person reads every book about changing their life and never changes a thing. It's all ideas, floating. The other works twelve-hour days, head down, and hasn't had a new thought in years. It's all motion, no meaning. Most of us lean one way or the other depending on the season. Today's sage is the son of Rabbi Judah the Prince, the man who gathered the Mishnah. He grew up surrounded by great scholars. And the first thing he tells us is that learning alone isn't enough.
screen: `ALL IDEAS, NO CHANGE.` → `ALL WORK, NO THOUGHT.` → `THE SON OF RABBI JUDAH.`

segments.voice: He's Rabban Gamaliel, the third of that name. His saying: beautiful is the study of Torah together with derekh eretz, because the effort of both keeps sin out of mind. Derekh eretz literally means the way of the land. Elsewhere it means good manners, but here it means earning a living, a trade, the ordinary work of the world. Why would the two together keep wrongdoing away? One reading is simple: a mind busy with learning and hands busy with work don't have much room left for trouble. But there's more. Learning keeps work honest, because you bring what you've learned to the market and the workshop. And work keeps learning honest, because you have to live the ideas with real people and real money. Then Gamaliel gives the warning side. Torah study without work, he says, ends in nothing and brings sin along with it. That's a strong line, and Jews have discussed the balance ever since. The Talmud records two sages who disagreed: one said a person should plow and plant in season and study too, and the other worried that if people are always plowing, when will the Torah get learned? Today, many Jews combine a job with regular study, and some communities support people who study full-time as a sacred calling. Each side reads this saying closely. What they share is Gamaliel's picture: learning and labor aren't enemies. They're two hands, and each keeps the other steady.
screen: `STUDY WITH DEREKH ERETZ.` · `TWO KINDS OF EFFORT KEEP SIN AWAY.` · `EACH KEEPS THE OTHER HONEST.` · `THE SAGES DEBATED THE BALANCE.` · then, large: `LEARNING AND LABOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pair one idea with one task. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've learned recently, anywhere, maybe even from one of these sayings. Careful words. Small ones count. Now think of the work waiting for you today, paid or unpaid. Where could that idea show up in it? In a meeting, a shift, a conversation with a customer or a child. Picture the two meeting. The bell holds the time.
Learning and labor. Rabban Gamaliel's pairing: Torah study with derekh eretz, the work of the world, each keeping the other honest.
Your line: learning and labor. Today, take one thing you've learned and use it at work, and take one question from your work back to something you study. Day two hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Many Jews combine a profession with regular Torah study, often a set time each day or week, while some communities support full-time study as a calling; both look to sayings like Avot 2:2.

what a scholar hears: derekh eretz, the way of the land, means a livelihood here, and the Talmud records sages who argued over the balance.

notes: Identifying the speaker as Rabban Gamaliel III, son of Rabbi Judah the Prince: standard; confirm the numbering.

The Talmud debate is Berakhot 35b: Rabbi Ishmael (combine work with study) and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai (if one plows in plowing season... what will become of Torah?). Sages are left unnamed here; confirm the paraphrase and whether to name them.
The present-day description (working and studying vs. full-time study communities) is deliberately balanced; a Keeper should check it is fair to both.
